## Architecture: seats, engine, characters, narrator

One deterministic engine sits at the center. Every language model touches the world only through a seat or a character, and every change it wants becomes an order the engine validates. The engine also holds the only copy of the game's state: the interface, the seats and any peers see only the views it releases.

&#91;embedded content: architecture · engine, seats, characters, narrator\]

Arrows down carry what the engine releases; arrows up carry requests the engine checks before anything changes.

**Seats.** Humans, leader models and script bots share one contract. In: a personal view (map, treasury, arrivals, envoy reports, audiences). Out: orders, letters and hires. The engine never knows who sits in a seat, which allows all-AI test games, swapping in a model when a human drops out, and fair comparisons between humans and models.

**Model allocation.**

| Role | Model | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaders | Sonnet 5.5 by default; Opus 5.5 for showcase and comparison games | Strongest reasoning where strategy matters, at a cost that allows many test games |
| Envoys, spies, candidates | Haiku 5.5 | Many calls per turn; they must stay in character, not plan grand strategy; fallible messengers suit the theme |
| Narrator | Sonnet 5.5 | Persona writing at creation and chronicles at the end, a few calls per game |

**Cost control.** Cache personas, system prompts and long histories (prompt caching); summarize character memory; cap messages per seat per turn; make the chronicle a toggle; use script bots for engine testing.

**Call size matters as much as call count.** In the first simulation the agents playing the kings used from about 26k to over 60k tokens an orders call over ten seasons, almost all of it journal and letters; the requests themselves grew from about 6k–8k to 11.5k–13.5k, and their fixed part, the rulebook, map and primer, from about 5k then to about 8k now (measured in item 1). Decided: older notes are summarized, so a king's memory of old betrayals survives, alongside a per-court ledger of promises. Which model writes the summaries is measured (see below). Candidates, to be weighed against a per-section breakdown of the request:

- older letters summarized to one line each, with the ledger keeping what was promised or threatened;
- the journal folding older notes as they leave the record, as characters already fold their memory;
- a "since you last acted" view instead of the whole picture, which matters more as sleep lengthens;
- terse state tables instead of prose, with the map's connections in the fixed part;
- ordering the request by stability, so the stable part is cached;
- lower effort for audience calls (built: one level below orders).

**Output is the other half** (decided 26 October 2026). A model writes only what the engine cannot: intentions, letters and judgements, never a report, a state table or a chronicle line the engine can put together from its own facts. An envoy who passes his king's words on as written, or an answer as given, writes nothing but his choice ("Languages"). Each job has its own cap on output, and replies carry no free-text reasoning fields, so a reply is as long as its decision. In unattended games between models, where nobody waits for a season, a provider's batch processing can run each season's simultaneous calls at a discount, half price on Anthropic's, with answers within a day.

**A cheaper model for condensing** (to be measured). Summaries could be written by a cheaper model than the seat's own, at the risk that a seat's memory drifts from its own voice. Keep the test cheap: have both models summarize the journals of a few recorded games and compare the summaries, a few dozen calls rather than new games, once model calls are allowed again after the build order ("No model games until the build order is done"). If it saves much at little loss, it becomes the default, and the setup menu lets a table choose otherwise; until then the seat's own model writes its summaries.

**The seat's model commits; a cheaper model handles what is light** (decided 18 October 2026, restated 20 October). The seat's own model, Sonnet by default, makes every commitment and every decision that matters: sealing a tablet, promising or paying land or large sums, detaining anyone, war and alliance, and whether he reopens his orders; what a woken king orders is his own model's too, unless the budget gives it to the script, which then only holds, defends and carries out what stands ("Minds follow what is at stake"). A cheaper model, Haiku by default, handles what is light: condensing a king's record once it measures as good enough ("A cheaper model for condensing"), and, playing the king from his record, routine audiences and light alerts (below). It never commits the king and never changes his orders, and wherever it is unsure it passes the matter on, so it errs toward the seat's own model: a false positive costs some tokens, a false negative costs a decision. The risk this guards against stays real: a king played by one model in one call and a weaker one in the next is less one mind, and the weaker calls are the ones rivals probe, which is why the cheaper model's answers commit nothing and item 6 measures what it passes on and what it missed.

**Routine audiences are answered by a cheaper model** (decided 19 October 2026, under the rule above). In routine audiences the cheaper model is the king, playing him from his journal, his ledger and his notes, so it is primed by the strategy his own model set, and it passes an audience on whenever the matter is important or it is unsure, erring toward passing it on. It reads the king's realm in brief as well as the envoy's words: in the second agent simulation, two of the three reopenings of orders came from the realm, not the message, and one of them probably saved Qadesh.

- **What it may do:** answer greetings, courtesy gifts, routine requests and renewals of peace, and give gifts in return, since an envoy sent home empty-handed is slighted. It is trusted to judge, as the king would, that his treasury is not to be emptied. As a hidden backstop there is a threshold on what the cheaper model gives in a season. It is not a cap: nothing is refused. An audience whose gift would pass it is handed to the seat's own model, which gives whatever it decides. The threshold scales with the king's wealth, as a share of his treasury as his own ledger shows it, not his true gold, so the routing never depends on a hidden fact such as debased gold; the share is set by balance tests.
- **What it may not do:** commit the king: seal, promise land, send large sums, detain anyone or change orders, which belong to the seat's own model.
- **What the engine passes on by itself:** anything it can see matters, judged only from what the king himself could see: a tablet shown or offered for sealing, a ransom demand, gold above a threshold, evidence of a broken tablet, troops at the border. A forged tablet is a tablet, so it always reaches the king's own model. The engine never routes on hidden facts, such as whether a tablet is forged, so being woken never tells a king that something is wrong.
- **Nothing tells the king.** Every answer is his own. The audience is recorded as the king's, with no mark of which model held it, and the rulebook and the seat view say nothing about models or routing. There is no court official or proxy answering for him. A wake names what is at the door ("an envoy with a tablet"), never why it was passed on.
- **One mind.** What he said and gave in those audiences is in his record like any other audience he held, so his next call carries on from it.

It serves sleeping model seats, and saves both the wake and the seat's own audience call (about 16k tokens in the replay); no model ever plays for a human seat, which may set standing answers only (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6c's review). Measure the saving, how often audiences are passed on, and whether rivals learn to exploit the cheaper answers. Two exploits in particular: a style tell, where a rival notices that a king's routine replies are shorter or plainer than his weighty ones and learns that dressing a request as important reaches the king's own model; and a leak, where the cheaper model, primed with the king's journal, lets slip plans he would keep.

**Light alerts go to the cheaper model too** (decided 20 October 2026). Not only envoys: every alert that reaches a sleeping king is routed by its weight.

- **Straight to the seat's own model:** anything about alliances, pacts, war, or forgery and evidence (a tablet offered, sealed, shown or questioned), and any alert that likely needs acting upon: foreign troops in his land or at his border, land or troops lost, a failed order, a ransom demand, a contract notice, a large gift.
- **To the cheaper model first:** alerts that are probably light, such as rumours, his own people's routine reports (an envoy home, word that his army has reached a place) and routine envoys. Playing the king from his record, it judges whether anything more is likely to need doing. It may acknowledge and answer within the limits of routine audiences, and it wakes the seat's own model whenever it sees anything that might matter, erring toward waking.
- **This is how a sleeping king follows his own campaign** without waking every season: word that his army has reached Qadesh arrives when someone brings it, the cheaper model reads it against the plan in his journal, and his own model is woken only if the plan needs changing.
- **It is not a wake of the king's own choosing.** The engine decides what is an alert, and judging an alert that has arrived is not asking to be woken ("No triggers of the seat's own"). It routes only on what the king himself could see, and every answer stays the king's own ("Nothing tells the king").

**Every model is the table's choice** (decided 19 October 2026). The setup menu sets a provider and a model for each job: kings, characters, the narrator, routine audiences, summaries and planning, each job a ladder of rungs ("Minds follow what is at stake"; "Built to outlive its models"). Any seat may override its job's choice, so Egypt can play on Opus and Hatti on another provider's model, which is how models are compared. The defaults are Sonnet for kings and the narrator, and Haiku for characters and the small jobs (summaries once "A cheaper model for condensing" is measured), but a table can give everything to Opus, or turn routine audiences off so that a seat's own model answers every envoy. Planning is off by default. When on, a strong model writes a king's plan into his journal at the start, once a year and when something large happens, a war declared, an ally lost or the capital threatened, and the king's own smaller model plays each season by that plan and may ask for a new one; the characters' strategy, written by a model at creation and again only when it changes, is the same idea ("How the strategy is made"). Planning is not the written strategy for model kings, which stays unbuilt ("A written strategy for model kings"): planning sets how a king plays the next seasons, not what kind of king he is. It lives in the game's own model layer, so it works with any provider. Anthropic's advisor tool, where a small model consults a larger one in the middle of a reply, does the same job but is not the way: the advisor reads the whole request at the larger model's rates, which for a king's request consulted every season costs nearly as much as playing on the larger model, and the newest advisors return their advice encrypted, where the log must show it. Whether planning plays as well for less is measured in the model games after the build order. The log records every choice, so games can be compared. The setup prices each model for the cost meter and the spending limit, and a model whose price the game does not know shows its cost as unknown, never as free, so the meter never quietly under-reports; a game with a spending limit does not start until every model it uses has a price, since a limit cannot hold against spending it cannot count (decided 27 October 2026; built in item 6c).

**Minds follow what is at stake** (decided 20 October 2026; revised 27 October 2026, its thresholds replaced, for every mind). A model call is spent where a model's judgement can change what happens, judged decision by decision, never by fixed thresholds on a power's size or wealth. It is one rule for every model-played mind, a Great King, a city-state, a vassal or a character, since no rule checks who a mind is ("Different data, same rules"), and it lives in the game's own model layer, so every rung can be any provider's model ("Built to outlive its models").

- **Three rungs for every job.** Each job is a ladder the table sets ("Every model is the table's choice"): the script, a small model and a large one, each rung naming any provider and model. By default kings and rulers climb from the script to Haiku to Sonnet, and characters from the script to Haiku, with Sonnet above for what is passed up. Routine audiences and light alerts are the ladder's first cases ("Routine audiences are answered by a cheaper model", "Light alerts go to the cheaper model too"), and what each rung may do stays as those entries and "The seat's model commits; a cheaper model handles what is light" set it: only a ruler's own model, the top rung, commits him.
- **What the script may do for a model-played mind.** It writes no words and starts nothing: it carries out standing orders and standing answers, holds, defends and supplies, and takes the routine steps of an errand, but never opens a war, seals or breaks a tablet, or takes an offer no standing answer covers. In full press words are always a model's, since script text has tells ("Script mode makes no model calls"): where the script or a standing answer decides something others will read, the small model words it in a phrasing call, from the clauses decided and the mind's voice, without its journal, the cheapest call there is.
- **What a call is worth.** The engine judges each decision a woken mind faces from what that mind itself could see, never from a hidden fact such as a forgery, true gold or the drawn last season. Three things count: what the decision can move, in the mind's own terms (a share of its gold, land or troops, its freedom or life, and what it carries for others, such as a tablet or a mission); how close the script's own choice is, which the engine works out anyway as the fallback (when its best option leads far, a model would rarely choose otherwise; when its options are close, or the matter is beyond its formulas, such as words that say more than their clauses, a model is worth more); and what the audits below have shown for that kind of decision. The scripts report how close their options are from item 18; until then the audits stand in for it, kind by kind (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6c's review). How they combine is a first guess, tuned in item 18.
- **A budget, spent where it buys the most.** The table sets what the game may cost (its spending limit) or what a season may cost. When the table turns pacing on (off by default until the first model games show what a season costs; decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6c's review), the engine paces itself from a limit, spreading what is left over the seasons the game can be expected to last by the table's own settings, never the drawn last season; in an open age, which has no expected end, the table also sets what a season may cost. Calls go to the decisions worth the most for their price, each to the rung that buys the most for it: the layer keeps a going rate, the worth per price its recent calls bought, makes a call when a decision clears it, and raises the rate when spending runs ahead of the pace and lowers it when spending lags, so a quiet season spends little, a crisis more, and no cut-off is set by hand. A cheaper model simply buys more calls. The price counted is the real one, cached tokens included, so a mind tends to stay on the model that holds its request in cache, with no rule for it, and a local model the table prices at nothing makes its rung free. What the budget cannot pay, the script decides where it may; the rest waits and grows in worth each season it waits. A court is never refused: an envoy is received the season he arrives, and the budget chooses only which model holds the court. A threat to any ruler's capital is always paid, from a reserve the budget keeps for it (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6c's review). A table comparing models gives each power a budget of its own, so one power's crisis does not spend another's calls. With pacing off, each job's model decides everything it decides today, and the limit only pauses the game.
- **Passing up and asking advice.** A lower rung that is unsure may pass a matter up whole, with its reason, as routine audiences already do, or keep it and ask the rung above for advice: it writes a brief of a few hundred tokens (the situation, its options and what it is unsure of), the stronger model answers the brief, never the whole request, and the lower rung decides. That is the advisor idea without the advisor tool's price ("Every model is the table's choice"). The advice goes into the mind's record with its own thoughts. When planning is on, the strong model writes the plan from a digest of the year, what the mind decided and what happened, rather than the whole record, and leaves standing answers with it.
- **Audits.** A small share of the decisions a lower rung takes (a setting; first guess, one in twenty) is also put, out of play, to the rung above. Its answer is never used: the log records whether the two differed and, by the script's own evaluation, how much it would have mattered. These rates feed the worth of each kind of decision as the game goes, starting from figures saved from earlier games or from first guesses, and the audits are paid from the budget. A table may set a target instead of a budget: how often a lower rung may decide otherwise than the rung above in a way that matters; the layer then spends what keeping to it takes.
- **Shadow scripts** (decided 27 October 2026). Beside every decision a model takes for a seat, the script decides too, out of play, since it costs nothing: the log records, by kind of decision, whether the two differed and, by the script's own evaluation, how much it would have mattered. Where script and model nearly always agree, or differ in ways that rarely matter, that kind of decision can go to the script; where they differ in ways that matter, it stays with the model. Audits check a cheaper model against a larger one; shadow scripts check the script against every model, for kings and characters alike. Built in item 18 with the scripts' margins, so it runs from the first model game, and read as "Script against model" under Tests says.
- **Standing answers.** A mind's model may leave standing answers, in any call and with every plan, for what arrives: an envoy, a gift, an offer, a request. They use the same engine-checkable vocabulary as scheduled orders ("Scheduled, conditional orders"): "return a courtesy gift with one of like value", "answer a brother's greeting in kind", "receive the tribute with thanks", or for a character "turn down any bribe below a sum" and "take any carrying job on roads he knows that pays above one". The engine carries them out for nothing, worded by a phrasing call in full press, and writes what they did into the mind's record. They act but never wake, so they cannot become a way to wake oneself ("No triggers of the seat's own"); their conditions read only what is known where they run; the hidden backstop on what is given in a season holds for them as for routine audiences; and whatever they do not cover goes up the ladder. They are the mind's own words given in advance, as an envoy carries a mandate, not a minister answering for him ("Dropped: the minister and the attention limit"). A human seat may set them too; they save calls and clicks, not strength, so script seats, which make no calls, need none.
- **One call per wake-up.** A woken mind settles everything waiting in one call: every envoy at its court, every alert and every offer. Reopening orders still runs the orders call ("What the replay showed").
- **Nothing tells anyone.** No mind learns which rung decided for it or for anyone else, and being given the strong model never signals that something matters ("Nothing tells the king"). Every decision, whichever rung took it, is in the mind's record as its own, so its next call carries on from it and it stays one mind. The log records the rung of every decision and why it was chosen, so a replay follows it exactly, and the spectator view shows it ("Who wrote it" under Spectator mode).
- **Presets.** The setup's presets (Free, Budget, Standard and Showcase) gain one more: Counsel, small models playing every mind, with the large ones planning, advising and taking what is passed up, and the narrator on the large model, since it writes each persona once and the chronicle at the end (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6c's review).
- **Measured** in the model games after the build order: what each rung decided, how often it passed up or asked, the audits' rates, the cost of a game against today's defaults, and whether rivals learn to tell the rungs apart (the style tell under "Routine audiences are answered by a cheaper model"). Built in item 6 (6b and 6c) for kings and characters; city-states and vassals join in item 11+, when they become powers, with nothing of their own.

**Logging and replay.** Every seed, order, prompt and output is logged, so any game can be replayed exactly and mined for the success signals ("Success criteria and test plan" under Tests, risks and references).
